stages.title: Economic systems
stages.hook: Every society must decide what to make, how to make it and who gets it. Who should decide: families, markets, or a government?
explain: An economic system is the way a society answers three questions: what to produce, how to produce it, and who gets it. Because resources are scarce, every society must answer them somehow.

In a traditional system, customs and habits guide choices, such as farming the way a community always has. In a market system, buyers and sellers decide through prices. In a command system, the government plans what is made. Most real countries have a mixed system, using markets for many goods and government for others such as roads or schools.

Economists and citizens disagree about the best mix. Markets can be flexible and reward new ideas, but may leave some people behind. Planning can aim at fairness or big projects, but may lack information about what people want. Each system has strengths and trade-offs.

example.q: In the island of Soma, the government says exactly how many shoes each factory must make. Which system is this closest to?
steps: Who decides what is made? The government.
That is the mark of a command system.
If shop owners and buyers decided through prices, it would be a market system.

analogies.home: A family may decide meals by tradition, by a parent's plan, or by each person buying their own snacks.
analogies.farm: A village may farm as elders always did, or by market prices, or by a state plan.
analogies.city: A city bus can be run by the government, while shops are run by owners.
analogies.sport: A league can have a coach picking the team, or fans and clubs trading players.

stages.mnemonic: WHAT, HOW, WHO: three questions every system must answer.
terms: The way a society decides what to produce, how, and for whom.
Prices and choices of buyers and sellers guide production.
The government plans production and distribution.
A system that uses both markets and government.

misc.wrong: A country is either fully market or fully planned.
misc.right: Almost all countries are mixed, with different amounts of government and market.

stages.limits: The labels are simplifications. Economists and voters disagree about the right balance, and the best mix can depend on a country's history and goals.

trip.prompt: Find the main types of economic system and an example country for each, noting that many are mixed.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the three basic questions every economy must answer?
o: What colour to paint the money
What goods and services to produce
How to produce them and with what
Who gets the things that are produced
questions.why: The core questions are what, how and for whom.

questions.q: In a market system, what mainly guides decisions?
o: Prices and choices of buyers and sellers
Orders from a single ruler and nothing else
Tradition and custom alone
Random chance and luck, with no other guide
questions.why: In markets, prices signal what is wanted and what is costly.

questions.q: A mixed economy is one where...
o: markets and government both play a role
every household makes everything it needs by itself
the economy has no use for money at all
only the oldest families are allowed to trade
questions.why: Mixed means both are used.

questions.q: In Karu, a community farms the same crops in the same way each year because that is the custom. This is closest to a...
o: traditional system
command system, since a planner decides each year
market system, since buyers set the price
mixed system, since the state and firms share the work
questions.why: Custom guides choices in a traditional system.

questions.q: Match each system to its main decision-maker.
pairs: A blend of government and markets
questions.why: Each system answers the three questions in a different way.

questions.q: Why does every society need an economic system at all?
o: Resources are scarce, so choices must be made
Money is too heavy to carry around
Shops would all have to close at night
People enjoy following rules about trade, whatever they cost
questions.why: Scarcity forces every society to decide how to use resources.

questions.q: A planner in a command system does not know how many people want umbrellas. What problem might arise?
o: Too many or too few umbrellas get made
Umbrellas become free, since nobody sets a price on them
Rain stops falling as soon as the plan is made
Umbrellas are banned from every shop and street
questions.why: Without price signals planners may lack information about wants.

questions.q: Give one strength and one weakness of a market system.
questions.model: A strength is that prices and choices let producers respond quickly to what people want. A weakness is that some people may be left behind or some needs may not be met.
questions.why: Markets are flexible but can leave inequality or gaps.

questions.q: Which statement is most accurate?
o: Most countries use a mix of markets and government
All countries are fully planned from the centre, with no markets
No country uses markets for anything it makes or sells
Governments take no part in any country's economy at all
questions.why: Real economies are mixed to different degrees.

questions.q: Put these in order from most government control to least in decisions about production.
questions.why: This runs from heavy to light government involvement. A fully free market is a theoretical idea.

panel.q: Two economists disagree about how big the government's role should be. What is the best view?
o: Both may be reasoning from different values and evidence, so trade-offs should be discussed
One of them must be lying about what the facts show
Economics has already settled the exact right size for government
Values play no part, since only numbers matter in the debate
panel.why: Policy choices involve both facts and values such as fairness and freedom.

panel.q: Why might a country use government for roads but markets for clothing?
panel.model: Roads are shared by everyone and hard to sell piece by piece, so government often provides them. Clothing can be sold to individuals, so markets can respond to different tastes.
panel.why: The suitable provider depends on the kind of good.

panel.q: Why is 'which system is best' hard to answer?
o: It depends on goals such as growth, fairness and freedom, and people weigh these differently
Because nobody has ever studied economic systems in any detail
Because all systems work in exactly the same way in practice
Because the answer is fixed by the amount of money in use
panel.why: Different goals lead to different judgments.

teach.model: Every society has to decide what to make, how to make it and who gets it. In a market system prices guide this, in a command system the government plans, and in a mixed system both are used. For example, a country may let shops sell clothes but have the government build roads.

points.ask: What does a society have to decide?
How does a market system decide?
Is any country purely one kind?

stages.title: Supply and demand
stages.hook: Why do mangoes cost less in the harvest season than when they are hard to find?
explain: Demand is how much of a good buyers want and can pay for at different prices. Usually, as the price rises, people buy less. This is the law of demand.
Supply is how much sellers are willing to sell at different prices. Usually, as the price rises, sellers offer more. This is the law of supply.

Prices change when supply or demand changes. A big harvest raises supply and tends to lower the price. If a food becomes popular, demand rises and the price tends to rise. These are tendencies, and other things can matter too.

example.q: A storm destroys many mango trees in the country of Velia. What tends to happen to the mango price, and why?
steps: The storm lowers the supply of mangoes.
Demand is about the same, so buyers compete for fewer mangoes.
Sellers can ask more, and the price tends to rise.
example.a: The price tends to rise, because supply falls while demand stays similar.

analogies.farm: A bumper harvest floods the market with grain, so prices tend to fall.
analogies.sport: A final match with few tickets and many fans pushes ticket prices up.
analogies.city: On a rainy day more people want taxis, so fares may rise.
analogies.music: A rare concert recording that many fans want can become expensive.

stages.mnemonic: Demand: buyers go down when price goes up. Supply: sellers go up when price goes up.
terms: How much buyers want and can pay for at each price.
How much sellers offer at each price.
Higher price usually means lower quantity demanded.
When buyers want more than is offered at the price.

misc.wrong: Prices are set only by what sellers decide.
misc.right: Prices come from the interaction of buyers and sellers, with supply and demand both mattering.

stages.limits: Supply and demand is a simplification. Real prices can also be affected by rules, expectations, or sellers with strong market power.

trip.prompt: Look at a supply and demand graph and find where the lines cross.

questions.q: The law of demand says that, other things equal, when the price rises...
o: buyers tend to buy less
buyers tend to buy more
sellers stop selling
nothing changes
questions.why: Higher price makes the good less attractive.

questions.q: Supply means...
o: how much sellers offer at each price
how much buyers want at each price
the price that money itself would fetch
how much a good weighs when it is delivered, at any price
questions.why: Supply comes from sellers.

questions.q: A heat wave makes many people want cold drinks. What tends to happen to demand?
o: It rises
It falls
It disappears
It stays zero
questions.why: More people want the good.

questions.q: A bumper rice harvest in the country of Taro. What tends to happen to rice prices, other things equal?
o: They fall
They rise sharply
They stay fixed
Rice disappears
questions.why: Supply rises so the price tends to fall.

questions.q: Match each event to its likely effect on price.
pairs: Price tends to go up as the good gets scarcer
questions.why: Prices respond to changes on either side.

questions.q: At 10 zeds each, 60 hats are demanded. At 20 zeds, 40 are demanded. By how many hats does quantity demanded fall when the price rises from 10 to 20?
questions.why: 60 − 40 = 20 fewer hats.

questions.q: A shortage means...
o: buyers want more than sellers offer at that price
sellers have more goods than buyers want at that price
the price has fallen to zero and nobody will pay
nobody wants the good at all at any price asked
questions.why: At a low price, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied.

questions.q: Why do ice cream prices often rise in summer? Use the words supply or demand.
questions.model: In hot weather more people want ice cream, so demand rises. If supply does not rise as much, the price tends to go up.
questions.why: Higher demand pushes prices up when supply is limited.

questions.q: Sellers produce more of a good when its price rises. Why?
o: Higher price makes extra output more worth the cost
They are told to by law whenever any price moves up
They dislike making profit and so work harder
They want customers to stop coming to the stall
questions.why: A higher price makes extra production more profitable.

questions.q: A new fashion makes a type of scarf popular while the number of scarves stays fixed. What is the most likely result?
o: The price rises
The price falls
Scarves disappear
No effect at all
questions.why: Demand rises while supply is fixed.

panel.q: Both supply and demand rise at the same time. What can we say for sure about the quantity traded?
o: It rises, but the price effect is unclear
The price must fall, because more of the good is on offer
The price must rise, because more people want it now
The quantity traded must fall, since two forces cancel out
panel.why: Quantity rises either way, but the price depends on which rise is larger.

panel.q: A government sets a maximum price on bread below the market price. Describe one possible result.
panel.model: At the lower price buyers want more bread while bakers want to supply less, so there may be a shortage and queues. The policy may still be used to help low-income families, which is a trade-off.
panel.why: Price ceilings can create shortages even if they help buyers who get the product.

panel.q: Why is it better to say 'prices tend to rise' than 'prices will rise'?
o: Other factors can also move prices
Prices never move at all in a real market
Economics is only guessing and has no firm ideas
Supply has no part in how prices are set at all
panel.why: Models describe tendencies. Real events have many influences.

teach.model: Demand is how much buyers want at each price and supply is how much sellers offer. When the price rises, buyers usually want less and sellers offer more. Prices change when either side changes. For example, after a big harvest there are lots of mangoes so the price tends to fall.

points.ask: What makes the price go up or down?

stages.title: Markets and prices
stages.hook: Nobody tells a town how many loaves of bread to bake each morning, yet shelves are usually full. How does that work?
explain: A market is any place or system where buyers and sellers meet to trade. It can be a street stall, a shop or a website.

Prices carry information. A high price tells sellers that a good is wanted and tells buyers it is costly. A low price signals the opposite. Prices also give incentives: sellers produce more when prices are high, buyers economise.

The equilibrium price is the price at which the quantity buyers want equals the quantity sellers offer. If the price is above it there is a surplus, so sellers cut prices. If it is below, there is a shortage and the price tends to rise.

example.q: At 5 coins, buyers want 50 loaves and bakers offer 80. What is there and which way does price tend to move?
steps: Compare: 80 offered is greater than 50 wanted.
That is a surplus of 30 loaves.
Bakers with unsold bread tend to cut the price.
example.a: A surplus of 30 loaves, so the price tends to fall.

analogies.city: A busy street market keeps prices close together because shoppers can compare stalls.
analogies.farm: If every farmer brings too many tomatoes, the price falls until buyers take them.
analogies.sea: Fish sold at the harbour gets cheaper late in the day if there are many unsold fish.
analogies.tech: Online shops can change prices many times a day as buyers click or leave.

stages.mnemonic: Surplus: sellers sigh and cut the price. Shortage: shoppers scramble and prices rise.
terms: The price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
More offered than buyers want at the price.
A reason to act in a certain way.

misc.wrong: Prices are just numbers shops pick at random.
misc.right: Prices carry information and give incentives about what is scarce and wanted.

stages.limits: Real markets can have rules, few sellers or poor information, which can stop prices from working smoothly. Some people also object to market outcomes on fairness grounds.

trip.prompt: Look for how prices act as signals in a market.

questions.q: Which is a market?
o: A website where people buy and sell
A kind of coin that is used only in shops
A thing you eat for lunch
A song people sing together
questions.why: A market is any place or system where buyers and sellers trade.

questions.q: At the equilibrium price...
o: quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
there is always a shortage of the good at that price
sellers always lose money at that price, whatever the cost
buyers pay nothing for the goods, and sellers give them away
questions.why: Equilibrium means the two quantities match.

questions.q: At 8 zeds a basket, buyers want 100 baskets but only 70 are offered. By how many baskets does demand exceed supply?
questions.why: 100 − 70 = 30, a shortage.

questions.q: In the shortage above, what tends to happen to the price?
o: It rises
It falls
It stays the same forever
It becomes zero
questions.why: Buyers compete for scarce baskets, pushing price up.

questions.q: A high price of a good tells sellers...
o: it is wanted or scarce, so producing more may pay
to stop all production, because the good is too dear
that nobody likes it, so output should be cut back
nothing at all, since prices carry no message to sellers
questions.why: Prices work as signals and incentives.

questions.q: A tomato seller ends the day with lots unsold. What is likely to happen tomorrow?
o: The seller may cut the price
The price will double
Tomatoes will become free forever
Buyers will vanish
questions.why: A surplus pushes prices down.

questions.q: Match the term to what it means.
pairs: More supplied than demanded at that price
More demanded than supplied at that price
Quantities match, no pressure to change
questions.why: These words describe how markets adjust.

questions.q: Explain in your own words how a price can tell sellers what to do.
questions.model: If the price rises, selling more becomes more profitable, so sellers tend to supply more. If the price falls, they may produce less.
questions.why: Prices signal scarcity and give incentives.

questions.q: Which market is most likely to have prices close together across sellers?
o: Many stalls selling the same goods where buyers compare
One seller far from anyone else, with no rivals nearby
A shop with a secret price list that buyers cannot see
The sale of a single unique painting, found only once
questions.why: Competition and comparison keep prices similar.

questions.q: A town floods and fresh water becomes scarce. What would a market price usually do?
o: Rise
Fall
Be exactly the same
Be zero
questions.why: Scarcity with demand unchanged pushes price up, though some places limit price rises for fairness.

panel.q: After a disaster, bottled water prices soar. Some people want a price limit; others want to let prices rise. Which statement is best?
o: Both sides raise valid points: limits may protect buyers, but high prices may attract more supply
Only one view can be right, so the others should be set aside
Prices do nothing in a crisis, so a limit has no effect
Water is never scarce, even after a disaster has struck
panel.why: This is a real policy trade-off between access and supply incentives.

panel.q: Why might markets fail to provide something even when people need it?
panel.model: Markets respond to demand backed by ability to pay. People in need who cannot pay, or goods that are shared by all, may not be provided by a market alone.
panel.why: Need is not the same as market demand.

panel.q: The price at which a market clears can be called 'efficient' by economists. Does this mean it is also 'fair'?
o: Not necessarily; efficiency and fairness are different ideas
Yes, always, since the market always settles on a fair price
Fairness means the same as efficiency in every case
They are two names for exactly one idea
panel.why: Efficiency is about using resources well, while fairness depends on values.

teach.model: A market is where buyers and sellers trade. If sellers offer more than buyers want, there is a surplus and prices tend to fall. If buyers want more than is offered, there is a shortage and prices tend to rise. They settle where the two match. For example, unsold tomatoes make the seller cut the price.

points.ask: What happens when there is too much?
And when there is too little?

stages.title: Production and consumption
stages.hook: A farmer grows wheat, a miller makes flour and a baker makes bread. Who 'produces' the bread you eat?
explain: Production is making goods and services. It uses resources called factors of production: land (natural resources), labour (people's work), capital (tools, machines, buildings) and enterprise (the people who organise and take risks).
Consumption is using goods and services to meet needs and wants. Households consume; firms produce and also use goods made by other firms.
Goods pass through stages from raw materials to the final product. Each stage adds value, which is why a loaf of bread costs more than the wheat it came from.

example.q: A farm sells wheat for 10 coins. A mill turns it into flour worth 15 coins. A bakery makes bread worth 25 coins. How much value does the bakery add?
steps: Bread is worth 25 coins.
The flour it started from was worth 15 coins.
Value added = 25 − 15 = 10 coins.

analogies.farm: Land, a farmer's labour, a plough and the farmer's plan together produce crops.
analogies.home: A family meal uses ingredients (land's gifts), cooking work, pots (capital) and someone organising the plan.
analogies.city: A bus company uses roads, drivers, buses and managers.
analogies.tech: A phone maker uses minerals, workers, factories and an entrepreneur's idea.

stages.mnemonic: LLCE: Land, Labour, Capital, Enterprise make what we eat and wear.
terms: Tools, machines and buildings used to produce.
The extra value created at one stage of production.

misc.right: In production, capital means tools, machines and buildings. Money is called financial capital.

stages.limits: Some economists add other factors such as knowledge or technology. Counting the value of unpaid work, like home care, is still debated.

trip.prompt: Find the factors of production and how they combine.

questions.q: Which is capital (in the production sense)?
o: A tractor
A farmer's work
A field of soil
The idea for a business
questions.why: Tools and machines are capital.

questions.q: Labour as a factor of production means...
o: people's work
a machine
natural resources
a loan
questions.why: Labour is human effort.

questions.q: Consumption means...
o: using goods and services
making goods in a factory or a field
saving coins for the future in a bank
building new factories and shops
questions.why: Consumers use what is produced.

questions.q: A mill buys wheat for 40 coins and sells the flour for 65 coins. What value does the mill add?
Which factor of production is 'land' in economics?
o: Natural resources such as soil, water and minerals
Only farms, and not the water or minerals
Only houses and the ground that they stand on
Money, since it is used to buy everything
questions.why: Land means all natural resources.

questions.q: Match the factor to an example.
pairs: A person starting a tailoring business
questions.why: Each factor plays a different role.

questions.q: Why does bread cost more than wheat?
o: Each stage of production adds value
Bread is magic and costs more for that reason alone
Wheat is free to everyone who asks for it
Shops dislike wheat and so charge less for it
questions.why: Milling and baking add value through work and resources.

questions.q: A village buys a water pump for farming. Explain how this changes production. Use the word capital.
questions.model: The pump is capital. It helps workers get more water to the crops with less effort, so output can rise.
questions.why: Capital makes labour more productive.

questions.q: Put these stages in order from raw material to final product.
items: Bread is bought by a family
questions.why: Goods move through stages to reach the consumer.

questions.q: A tailor sews shirts for sale and also buys thread. In this case the thread is...
o: an input to production
a final consumer good only
a service
land
questions.why: Thread is used up making the shirts.

panel.q: Home cooking and childcare by family members are not sold on markets. How should an economist think about them?
o: They create real value, though they are hard to measure in money
They have no value, since no money changes hands
They are always counted exactly in every national total
They are a kind of capital, like a machine or a tool
panel.why: Unpaid work has value but is often missing from market measures.

panel.q: Why can two farms with the same land and workers produce different amounts?
panel.model: They may differ in tools, skills, methods or the quality of soil and water, so the same number of workers can produce different outputs.
panel.why: Productivity depends on more than quantity of inputs.

panel.q: A factory replaces some workers with machines. Which statement is fair?
o: Output may rise but some workers may need new jobs, so there are benefits and costs
It is always good for every single person, so no one loses
It is always bad for every single person, so no one gains
Nothing changes in output or in jobs after the switch
panel.why: Technology can raise production while changing who has work.

teach.model: Production means making goods and services using land, labour, capital and enterprise. Consumption means using them. Each stage of production adds value. For example, wheat becomes flour and then bread, and each step adds value.

points.ask: What do you need to produce something?

stages.title: Opportunity cost
stages.hook: You have a free Saturday. You can play football or visit your cousin. Whatever you pick, what do you lose?
explain: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best choice that you give up when you decide. It is not just money: time counts too.

If a farmer plants beans on a field, the opportunity cost is the best other use of that field, such as maize. Opportunity cost makes the idea of 'free' tricky: a free afternoon still has a cost if you could have done something else with it.
Thinking about opportunity cost helps people, firms and governments compare options, but it needs honest guesses about what the next best option is worth.

example.q: Ravi has one hour. He can tutor a friend for 6 coins or mow a lawn for 8 coins. He chooses mowing. What is his opportunity cost?
steps: Next best option: tutoring, worth 6 coins.
Opportunity cost is the value of the best option given up.
So it is 6 coins, not 8.

analogies.home: Choosing to watch TV costs you the homework time you could have used.
analogies.farm: A field used for cattle cannot also grow wheat at the same time.
analogies.sport: Training for running for an hour means not training swimming in that hour.
analogies.city: A city that builds a car park cannot use that land for a park.

stages.mnemonic: Opportunity cost = the road not taken.
terms: Value of the best alternative given up.
Giving up some of one thing to get more of another.
A different option you could choose.

misc.wrong: Opportunity cost is all the options you gave up.
misc.right: It is the value of the single next best option you gave up.

stages.limits: The value of an alternative is often a guess, and people value things differently, so opportunity costs are not always exact numbers.

trip.prompt: Find the example on the page and name the thing given up.

questions.q: Opportunity cost is...
o: the value of the next best option you give up
the price printed on the label
all your costs added up for the year
the cheapest option out of those you could choose
questions.why: It is the best alternative forgone.

questions.q: Lena spends Saturday at a concert. She could have earned 20 coins working. The opportunity cost of the concert includes...
o: the 20 coins she could have earned
nothing, since it was her own day to spend
the ticket price only, and not her time
all her future earnings, for the rest of her life
questions.why: Time has a cost: the best alternative use.

questions.q: A farmer can grow maize worth 500 coins or beans worth 420 coins on a field. She grows maize. What is the opportunity cost in coins?
questions.why: The next best choice is beans, worth 420 coins.

questions.q: A worker earns 12 coins per hour. She spends 3 hours at a free workshop instead of working. What did she give up in coins from earnings?
A town builds a library on its last empty lot. Which is an opportunity cost?
o: The park or market that could have been built there
The library itself, which the town has now built
The books that are placed on its shelves
The name of the librarian who will work there
questions.why: What the lot could have been used for instead is the cost.

questions.q: Match each choice to the opportunity cost.
pairs: The best other crop on that land
The next best thing the money could buy
The school it could have funded
questions.why: In each case the cost is the next best alternative given up.

questions.q: Is anything truly 'free' in economics?
o: Not usually: using time or resources has an opportunity cost
Yes, everything is free if no money is handed over
Only food is ever truly free
Only education is ever truly free
questions.why: Even when no money is paid, the time and resources used could have been used otherwise.

questions.q: Explain why two people can have different opportunity costs for the same choice.
questions.model: The opportunity cost is the best alternative given up, and people have different alternatives and value them differently, so the same choice can cost them different things.
questions.why: Alternatives are personal.

questions.q: A school has money for either a new playground or new books, not both. It chooses books. The opportunity cost is...
o: the playground
the books, which the school bought
both the playground and the books together
neither one, since the money was spent only once
questions.why: The playground is the next best option forgone.

questions.q: Why does opportunity cost help in decisions?
o: It shows what you really give up when you choose
It removes all choices, so nothing is left to decide
It makes every option look equal, whatever it costs
It guarantees that the choice will turn out well
questions.why: It highlights trade-offs hidden behind prices.

panel.q: A government can spend on a hospital or a road. Which statement shows careful thinking?
o: Compare what each would give and be honest about what is lost, recognising people may value outcomes differently
The hospital is always the better use of the money
The road is always the better use of the money
Spend on neither, since any choice is risky
panel.why: Opportunity cost shows the trade-off but values decide the choice.

panel.q: Why is the opportunity cost of staying in school often not just the fees?
panel.model: Besides fees, the student gives up the income they might have earned working, so time and earnings count as part of the cost.
panel.why: Opportunity cost includes forgone earnings.

panel.q: Sam says: 'The concert was free, so it cost me nothing.' What is a good reply?
o: It cost your time and what you could have done with it
You are right, there is no cost at all, since nothing was paid
Free things always cost double what others do
Time has no value, so it cannot be a cost
panel.why: Opportunity cost includes time.

teach.model: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best thing you give up when you make a choice. If you spend an hour playing, you cannot use that hour for homework. For example, a farmer who grows maize on a field gives up the beans she could have grown.

stages.title: Income and spending
stages.hook: Two families both earn 100 coins a week but one always runs out first. What could explain that?
explain: Income is the money a person or household receives, from wages, selling things, gifts or other sources. Spending is money paid out.
Spending can be on needs, wants, taxes or paying back loans. What is left after spending can be saved. If spending is more than income, a person must use savings or borrow.
Households can compare fixed costs (like rent, which stays the same) and variable costs (like snacks, which change). Tracking both helps people plan.

example.q: Nadia earns 200 coins a month. Rent is 80, food is 60, transport is 20 and other spending is 30. How much is left to save?
steps: Income − spending = 200 − 190.
That is 10.

analogies.home: A family jar for food money shows how income flows out into spending.
analogies.farm: A farmer's income comes after harvest, so spending must be planned across the year.
analogies.city: A bus pass is a fixed cost; ice cream is variable.
analogies.sport: A club has income from tickets and spending on kit and travel.

stages.mnemonic: In minus Out equals what is left: Income − Spending = Saving.
terms: A cost that stays the same each period.
A cost that changes with use.

misc.wrong: Earning more always means you can save more.
misc.right: If spending rises just as much, nothing is left to save. What counts is the gap between income and spending.

stages.limits: Incomes vary a lot and can be uncertain, for example for farmers or casual workers. Saving is easier when income is steady.

trip.prompt: Find the different types of income, such as wages and profit.

questions.q: Income is...
o: money received
money spent
money lost
money borrowed only
questions.why: Income is what comes in.

questions.q: Which is a fixed cost?
o: Monthly rent of 80 coins
Ice cream bought on a hot day
A surprise gift
A bus ride you chose to take
questions.why: Rent is the same each month.

questions.q: Income is 150 coins. Spending is 120 coins. How many coins are saved?
Omar earns 18 coins per hour and works 25 hours. What is his income in coins?
A family spends more than its income for three months. What must happen?
o: They use savings or borrow
Nothing
Prices drop
Their income grows by itself
questions.why: The gap must be covered somehow.

questions.q: Match each item.
questions.why: These are parts of a household budget.

questions.q: Kofi's income rises from 300 to 360 coins, a rise of 20%. His spending rises from 280 to 350 coins. What happens to his saving?
o: It falls from 20 to 10
It rises from 20 to 30
It stays at 20, since income and spending both rose
It falls to zero
questions.why: Saving = income − spending: 300−280=20, 360−350=10.

questions.q: Why can a household with low income still have good money habits?
questions.model: Good habits such as planning, paying for needs first and saving even a little can help at any income, though a very low income makes this much harder.
questions.why: Habits matter, but income limits what is possible.

questions.q: Put the money flow in order.
questions.why: Plan needs first, then wants, then what is left can be saved.

questions.q: A farmer earns most income at harvest. What is a sensible way to plan?
o: Spread the money over the year, setting some aside
Spend it all at once as soon as it arrives
Never spend any of it during the year
Hide it from the family so it cannot be used
questions.why: Irregular income needs planning across months.

panel.q: Two households have the same income but different spending patterns. Which statement is fair?
o: Differences may reflect needs, such as medical costs, as well as choices
The one that spends more is always wasteful
The one that saves more is always wise
Income alone explains every difference in spending
panel.why: Circumstances differ, so judging people without context is unfair.

panel.q: Why might a shop owner want to know the difference between fixed and variable costs?
panel.model: Fixed costs must be paid whatever is sold, while variable costs change with sales. Knowing both helps set prices and see how much to sell to make a profit.
panel.why: It helps with pricing and planning.

panel.q: Which is the best definition of saving?
o: Income not spent on current consumption
Anything you own, such as a house or a car
Money borrowed from a lender
Money you owe to someone else
panel.why: Saving is income minus consumption.

teach.model: Income is the money you get and spending is the money you pay out. What is left over is saving. If you spend more than you earn, you must use savings or borrow. For example, if I earn 200 coins and spend 190, I save 10.

stages.title: Saving and banking
stages.hook: If you leave coins in a bank, why might the bank pay you extra later?
explain: A bank keeps money safe. It also lends part of the money it holds to other people and firms, and charges them interest for the loan. It pays savers a smaller amount of interest for the use of their money.

Interest is money paid for using money. With simple interest, you earn the same amount each year on the original amount. With compound interest, you earn interest on both your savings and the interest you have already earned, so growth speeds up over time.
Banks lend and borrowers repay. Savings can be lost in a failed bank, which is why many countries have rules and protections. Saving does not guarantee growth if prices rise faster than interest.

example.q: Mia saves 1,000 zeds at 5% simple interest per year. How much interest does she earn in 3 years?
steps: One year: 5% of 1,000 = 50.
Three years: 3 × 50 = 150.
Total interest is 150 (balance 1,150).

analogies.nature: A snowball rolling downhill picks up more snow as it grows, like compound interest.
analogies.farm: A seed grows into a plant that makes more seeds.
analogies.home: A jar in the bank gets a small gift for letting the bank use the coins.
analogies.city: A bank is like a town pool of savings that others can borrow from.

stages.mnemonic: Simple interest is a straight line; compound interest is a snowball.
terms: Money paid for the use of money.
Interest on the original amount only.
Interest on the original amount and past interest.
Money borrowed that must be repaid, usually with interest.

misc.wrong: Money in a bank always grows in real buying power.
misc.right: If prices rise faster than the interest rate, buying power can fall.

stages.limits: Interest rates differ across banks and times. This lesson gives no advice on where to save.

trip.prompt: Look at how compound interest grows over time compared with simple interest.

questions.q: A bank pays interest to savers because...
o: it uses their money to lend to others
it enjoys giving gifts to the people it knows
savers are always rich and need more money
the law forbids banks from making any profit
questions.why: Banks lend deposits and share part of the earnings.

questions.q: 500 zeds earns 4% simple interest per year. How much interest after 1 year?
2,000 zeds earns 5% simple interest per year. How much interest in 4 years?
100 zeds earns 10% compound interest per year. What is the balance after 2 years in zeds?
Compared with simple interest, compound interest over many years gives...
o: more growth, since interest earns interest
less growth, since the interest is smaller each year
the same growth, whatever the type of interest
no growth at all after the first year
questions.why: Interest on interest adds up.

questions.q: Match the term to its meaning.
questions.why: Basic banking words.

questions.q: Prices rise by 6% in a year but a savings account pays 2%. What happens to buying power?
o: It falls
It rises
It is unchanged
It doubles
questions.why: Money grows 2% but prices grow 6%, so you can buy less.

questions.q: Why does a bank charge a higher interest rate on loans than it pays on savings?
questions.model: The difference lets the bank cover its costs and the risk that some loans are not repaid and still make a profit.
questions.why: The gap between rates funds the bank's work and risk.

questions.q: Why is it generally safer to keep savings in a regulated bank than under a mattress?
o: It reduces risk of theft or loss and may earn interest
Banks never fail, so the money cannot be lost
Mattresses are illegal places to keep any money
Interest is guaranteed to always beat rising prices
questions.why: Banks add safety and interest, though no option is risk-free.

questions.q: Which is a good habit for a young saver?
o: Set a goal and save regularly
Spend first and save what is left, if any
Never plan
Keep all savings in one place with no thought
questions.why: Regular saving builds up over time.

panel.q: Why is starting to save early often helpful under compound interest?
o: Interest has more time to build on itself
Banks give a bonus to children who start early
Money doubles every single year without fail
Interest rates are always high at any age
panel.why: Time lets compounding work longer, though returns are not guaranteed.

panel.q: A friend says 'banks just take people's money'. Give a balanced reply.
panel.model: Banks keep money safe and lend it so others can buy homes or start businesses, and they pay savers interest. They also charge fees and make profits, and they can fail, so rules and care matter.
panel.why: Banks give benefits and have costs.

panel.q: Borrowing money for a business that earns more than the interest cost can be useful. What is the main risk?
o: The business may not earn enough to repay
The loan is always free, so there is no risk
Interest is negative, so the borrower earns a gain
Banks never lend to a business, so a loan is not possible
panel.why: Loans must be repaid even if plans fail.

teach.model: A bank keeps your money safe and uses it to lend to others. It pays you interest for letting it use your money. With compound interest you earn interest on your interest, so savings grow faster over time. For example, 100 zeds at 10% a year becomes 110 and then 121.

points.ask: What does a bank do with money?
Why does it pay you extra?

stages.title: Trade and specialisation
stages.hook: One country grows bananas well and another makes machines well. Could both be better off if they trade?
explain: Specialisation means focusing on one kind of work or product. People, firms and countries who specialise can get better and faster at it.

Trade lets each side exchange what it makes well for what others make well. Even if one side is better at everything, trade can still help both if they focus on what they give up least. This idea is called comparative advantage.
Trade brings more variety and lower prices, but some jobs and firms can lose from competition. Societies argue about how to share the gains and help people who lose.

example.q: In one day, Ana can make 4 baskets or 2 mats. Ben can make 1 basket or 1 mat. Who has the lower opportunity cost for baskets?
steps: Ana: 4 baskets cost 2 mats, so 1 basket costs 0.5 mat.
Ben: 1 basket costs 1 mat.
Ana gives up less per basket (0.5 vs 1).
example.a: Ana, who gives up only 0.5 mat per basket

analogies.farm: One farm grows coffee and another dairy; they swap and both have both.
analogies.sport: A team has specialist goalkeepers and strikers instead of everyone doing everything.
analogies.city: A city of bakers, doctors and drivers can offer many services because each focuses.
analogies.tech: Some countries make chips, others assemble phones, and both gain.

stages.mnemonic: Do what you give up least, then trade for the rest.
terms: Focusing on a particular task or product.
Producing something at a lower opportunity cost.

misc.wrong: A country that is better at everything gains nothing from trade.
misc.right: Even then, trade can help both if each focuses on where its opportunity cost is lower.

stages.limits: Trade can hurt some workers and industries even if the country gains overall. People disagree about how to balance this.

trip.prompt: Find the classic example of two goods and two countries.

questions.q: Specialisation means...
o: focusing on one type of work or product
doing everything for yourself, with no trade
avoiding trade with other people
working fewer hours in the day
questions.why: Specialists focus.

questions.q: Why do people trade?
o: Both sides can end up better off
To lose money on purpose and gain nothing
Because the law forces everyone to trade
To avoid doing any work at all
questions.why: Voluntary trade can benefit both.

questions.q: An export is a good that is...
o: sold to another country
bought from another country
made in a home
kept forever
questions.why: Exports leave the country.

questions.q: In a day, Kira makes 6 pots or 3 lamps. What is her opportunity cost of one lamp in pots?
questions.why: 3 lamps cost 6 pots, so 1 lamp costs 2 pots.

questions.q: Tom can make 5 shirts or 10 hats in a day. What is his opportunity cost of one shirt in hats?
questions.why: 5 shirts = 10 hats, so one shirt = 2 hats.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
questions.why: Trade words fit together.

questions.q: Maya can bake 10 cakes or sew 5 scarves in a day. Joe can bake 4 cakes or sew 4 scarves. Who should bake?
o: Maya, because she gives up less per cake (0.5 scarf vs 1)
Joe, because he is better at sewing
Neither, since they should not trade
Both must sew, and neither should bake
questions.why: Maya's opportunity cost of a cake is 5/10 = 0.5 scarf; Joe's is 1.

questions.q: Explain one benefit and one possible cost of trade between countries.
questions.model: Trade gives more choice and often lower prices. But some local firms and workers may lose from the competition, so societies must consider how to help them.
questions.why: There are gains and adjustment costs.

questions.q: A tiny island has few resources. How could trade help it?
o: It can buy what it cannot produce and sell what it can
It cannot trade, since it is too small
It must make everything itself on the island
Trade makes it poorer, so it should avoid it
questions.why: Trade extends choices beyond local resources.

questions.q: Order the steps of gaining from trade.
items: Each side finds what it gives up least to make
questions.why: Compare costs, specialise, trade, gain.

panel.q: A country says: 'We are better at making everything, so we should not trade.' What is the best response?
o: Comparative advantage shows gains can exist anyway
They are right, since being best at all things means no gain
Trade is not allowed between such countries
Being better at everything means trade has no cost
panel.why: What matters is relative, not absolute, opportunity cost.

panel.q: Why might a government protect a local industry from imports, and what is a trade-off?
panel.model: A government may want to protect jobs, new industries or national security. The trade-off is that consumers can face higher prices and fewer choices, and others may respond with their own barriers.
panel.why: Protection has benefits and costs.

panel.q: Heavy specialisation can be risky because...
o: if that product's price falls or is disrupted, the whole area suffers
specialists never learn anything new about their work
trade cannot happen between specialised areas
it always raises opportunity cost for every worker
panel.why: Dependence on a single product increases exposure to shocks.

teach.model: Specialisation means focusing on what you do best or give up least. Then people or countries trade for the rest, so both end up with more. For example, one farm grows coffee, another makes milk, and they swap.

stages.title: Basic business economics
stages.hook: A girl sells lemonade for 2 coins a cup. How can she tell whether the stall is really making money?
explain: A business sells goods or services to earn money. Revenue is the money it receives from sales: price × quantity. Costs are what it pays to run, such as ingredients, rent and wages. Profit = revenue − costs.
If revenue is less than costs, the business makes a loss. The break-even point is where revenue equals costs. To keep going, owners must make enough sales or lower costs.
Businesses also take risks. Owners are called entrepreneurs when they start a new idea. Good businesses watch costs, set prices carefully and listen to customers.

example.q: Leila sells 40 cups of lemonade at 2 coins. Her costs are 50 coins. What is her profit?
steps: Revenue = 40 × 2 = 80.
Costs = 50.

analogies.farm: A farmer's revenue is from selling crops; seed and tools are costs.
analogies.sport: A club earns from tickets and pays for players and the stadium.
analogies.city: A cafe covers rent and wages from the cups it sells.
analogies.tech: An app earns from users and pays for servers and designers.

stages.mnemonic: Profit = Revenue − Costs: what comes in minus what goes out.
terms: Money spent to run the business.
A person who starts and runs a business, taking risks.

misc.wrong: A high revenue means a high profit.
misc.right: Profit depends on costs too. A business can have large sales and still make a loss.

stages.limits: Businesses may also care about goals like jobs, quality or helping the community, not only profit.

trip.prompt: Find how revenue, costs and profit are linked.

questions.q: Profit equals...
o: revenue minus costs
revenue plus costs
costs minus revenue
price only
questions.why: Profit is what remains after costs.

questions.q: A stall sells 30 snacks at 4 coins each. What is its revenue?
Revenue is 200 coins and costs are 150 coins. What is the profit?
A baker has costs of 90 coins and sells cakes at 6 coins each. How many cakes must she sell to break even?
A business has revenue 80 and costs 100. This is a...
o: loss of 20
profit of 20
break-even
profit of 180

questions.q: An entrepreneur is someone who...
o: starts a business and takes risks
only works for other people for a wage
lends money for others to use
sets the taxes that firms must pay
questions.why: Entrepreneurs organise and risk starting something new.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
questions.why: Business arithmetic.

questions.q: A shop raises its price but sells fewer items. Explain why profit might go up or down.
questions.model: Each item earns more, but fewer are sold. Profit rises if the extra earned per item outweighs the sales lost, and falls if not, so it depends on how much sales drop.
questions.why: Price and quantity move in opposite directions.

questions.q: Why does a business need to know its costs?
o: To set prices and see if it can make a profit
To avoid customers who ask for lower prices
To hide its income from other people
It does not need to know, since costs do not affect prices
questions.why: Costs set the minimum viable price.

questions.q: A stall's lemons cost more this week. What are its options?
o: Raise the price, cut costs elsewhere or accept a lower profit
Ignore the change and hope for the best
Close the stall at once, always, in every case
Stop counting and keep the old price whatever happens
questions.why: Businesses adjust prices or costs.

panel.q: A business makes a small profit but treats its workers unfairly. Which comment is most balanced?
o: Profit is one measure; fairness, quality and community effects also matter to many people
Only profit matters, so the way workers are treated is not important
Profit is always evil, so no business should aim for it
Workers do not matter to a business, so their treatment is not a concern
panel.why: People hold different views of business goals.

panel.q: Why do some new businesses fail even when many people like the product?
panel.model: Even popular products fail if costs are too high or prices too low to make a profit, if cash runs out, or if competition is strong.
panel.why: Liking is not the same as covering costs.

panel.q: A cafe opens but customers are few at first. Which statement shows good thinking?
o: Check costs, prices and marketing, and be ready for risk
Blame the customers for not coming to the cafe
Ignore the numbers and carry on as before
Shut the cafe at once, since it did not start well
panel.why: Careful analysis helps entrepreneurs adapt.

teach.model: Revenue is the money a business gets from sales. Costs are what it pays out. Profit is revenue minus costs. If costs are bigger, it makes a loss. For example, selling 40 cups at 2 coins gives 80 coins; with costs of 50 the profit is 30.
